cues.x: Ultra-Processed People, by Chris van Tulleken.
Let me start you in a kitchen in London, late at night, with a doctor standing over a plastic tray.
Chris van Tulleken is an infectious diseases physician at University College London Hospital.
He has a doctorate in molecular virology.
He has spent years making science programmes for the BBC, and he is, by any standard, a man who knows what a healthy diet is and has the resources and the knowledge to eat one.

And on this particular night, near the end of a four week experiment, he is eating a ready meal out of a plastic tray at eleven o'clock at night, standing up, not hungry, not enjoying it, and unable to stop.
That moment is the hinge of the whole book, because of what he says about it afterwards.
He does not describe it as a lapse of willpower.
He describes it as the predictable output of a system that had been operating on him for four weeks exactly as designed.
Here is what he had done.
For a BBC documentary, and with a research team at University College London monitoring him, van Tulleken agreed to eat a diet made up of eighty percent ultra-processed food for one month.
He did not choose eighty percent to be shocking.
He chose it because that is roughly what one in five people in the United Kingdom actually eats, every day, for their whole lives.
He was not eating an absurd diet.
He was eating a very ordinary one.
He had scans, blood tests, hormone measurements and psychological assessments before and after.
In four weeks he gained about six kilograms, a little over a stone.
He worked out that if he had continued at that rate for a year he would have roughly doubled his body weight.
His hunger hormones went haywire: the signals that are supposed to tell your brain you have eaten stopped behaving properly, so he stayed hungry after meals in a way he had not been before.
He was constipated, he slept badly, he developed anxiety, he felt about a decade older, and he described a persistent low-grade misery.
And then the finding that unsettled him most.

When they compared brain scans before and after, they found that new functional connections had appeared, strengthening the links between the parts of his brain that drive automatic, habitual behaviour and the parts that handle reward and desire.
In four weeks.
That is the architecture you see described in the literature on addiction.
He had, in a month, partially rewired the relationship between wanting food and choosing food.
So he wrote this book to answer a question that had stopped being academic: what exactly is this stuff, why does it do this, and why is it now most of what the English-speaking world eats?
Before we go further, a word about the author, because it matters to how the book reads.
Van Tulleken has an identical twin brother, Xand, who is also a doctor and with whom he has made television for years.
Xand spent a long period living with obesity, and the two of them, genetically identical, ended up in very different bodies.
That fact sits underneath the whole book.
If your genes are identical and your outcomes are not, then the explanation is in the environment, and Chris van Tulleken spends four hundred pages describing that environment.
It is worth sitting with the texture of that month, because the details are more revealing than the headline numbers.
He was not eating exotically.

He ate the things people eat: cereal and long-life milk in the morning, a supermarket meal deal at lunch, a ready meal or a takeaway in the evening, snacks and fizzy drinks and squeezy fruit pouches in between.
The diet was, in his description, monotonous and beige and entirely unremarkable, which is exactly the point.
The most striking thing he reports is not that it was disgusting.
It is that within about ten days it stopped feeling like an experiment at all.
It became normal.
His desire adapted.
Food that had initially seemed too sweet began to taste correct, and fruit began to seem underwhelming.
The people around him noticed before he did.

He describes his daughter, small at the time, being suddenly fascinated by the packets arriving in the house, which he found more disturbing than any of his own test results, because it showed him how fast the preference is installed.
He describes waking at night.
He describes the sensation of having eaten and being hungry ten minutes later, which is not a moral failing but a hormone measurement, and they had the measurement.

And he describes the peculiar, low-grade sadness of the last week, when he could feel that he was going to continue eating this way regardless of the fact that he had signed a piece of paper agreeing to stop at the end of the month.

When it ended, the weight came off over a few weeks and most of the markers returned toward normal, which he is careful to note, because the acute experiment says nothing about what forty years of the same diet would do to a person who never gets a stop date.
That is the population-level question, and none of us are in a metabolic ward.
Now.
What actually is ultra-processed food?
Because this is not a vague wellness word.
It is a technical category with a specific origin story, and the story is genuinely good.

In the late nineteen nineties and early two thousands, a Brazilian professor of nutrition and public health named Carlos Monteiro was working through decades of Brazilian household food purchasing data.
He was looking at what families actually bought, year by year, as the country changed.
And he found something that made no sense under the standard model of nutrition.
Brazilian households were buying less sugar.
They were buying less salt.
They were buying less cooking oil.
Year after year, the purchase of the things nutritionists blamed for obesity was falling.
And obesity was rising, fast.
Under the prevailing nutrient-based way of thinking, that is close to a paradox.
Monteiro sat with it and eventually saw the resolution, which is obvious once stated and was invisible before.
Families were buying less sugar and oil because they were doing less cooking.
The sugar and the oil had not left their diets.
They had simply moved.
They were now arriving pre-installed inside industrially manufactured products, along with a great many other things.
The relevant variable was not the nutrient.
It was who did the processing, and how far it went.
That insight produced the NOVA classification, which is the framework the whole field now argues about, and it sorts food by degree and purpose of processing rather than by nutrient content.
There are four groups.
Group one is unprocessed or minimally processed food.
An apple, a chicken breast, dried beans, plain frozen peas, milk, oats, a bag of rice.
Things that have had bits removed, been dried, chilled, frozen or ground, but nothing added.
Group two is processed culinary ingredients.
Oil, butter, sugar, salt, vinegar, honey.
These are extracted from group one foods and are not usually eaten alone.
They are what you cook with.
Group three is processed food.
Take group one, add group two, and you get bread from a bakery, cheese, tinned fish in oil, salted nuts, home-canned tomatoes, most traditionally made things.
Processing here is old, usually for preservation or palatability, and generally involves ingredients you would recognise.
Group four is ultra-processed food.
And Monteiro's definition is not about how many steps are involved or how much machinery.
It is about what goes in.

Ultra-processed foods are industrial formulations made mostly or entirely from substances extracted from foods or synthesised in laboratories, typically containing few if any intact group one ingredients, and, crucially, containing additives whose function is to make a cheap, industrially degraded product look, feel, smell and taste like food.
Emulsifiers.
Non-sugar sweeteners.
Colours.
Flavourings.
Flavour enhancers.
Thickeners.
Humectants.
Bulking agents.
Anti-caking agents.
Modified starches.
Protein isolates.
Van Tulleken offers a working shortcut for the supermarket, and it is the most quoted line in the book.
If it is wrapped in plastic and contains at least one ingredient you would not normally find in a domestic kitchen, it is ultra-processed food.
That is not a perfect rule and he knows it.
But it will get you most of the way there, standing in an aisle, in about four seconds.
The category is bigger than people expect, and this is where the book becomes uncomfortable.
It is not just crisps and fizzy drinks and confectionery.
It is most supermarket sliced bread.
Most breakfast cereal, including the ones with a picture of a field on the box.
Most flavoured yoghurt.
Most plant milks.
Most protein bars.
Most meal replacement shakes.
Most ready meals, including the healthy ranges.
Most sausages and reformed meat products.
Most sauces.
A great deal of what is marketed as diet food, and a great deal of what is marketed as health food, precisely because low-fat and low-sugar reformulation requires more additives, not fewer.
And the quantity is the part that stops people.
In the United Kingdom and the United States, ultra-processed food makes up roughly sixty percent of the average diet by calories.
For adolescents it is higher, in many surveys around eighty percent.
These two countries are at the top of the global table.
This is not a fringe portion of the food supply.
It is the food supply.
Now, at this point, a sensible person asks the obvious question.
Is any of this actually about processing, or is it just that these foods happen to be full of sugar, salt and fat, and we have known those are a problem for fifty years?

The answer to that question is the most important experiment in the book, and it was run by a physicist turned metabolic researcher named Kevin Hall at the National Institutes of Health in the United States.
Hall, incidentally, went in as a sceptic.
He thought the ultra-processed idea was probably imprecise and unscientific, and he designed the trial expecting to find not much.
Here is what he did.
Twenty adults were admitted to a metabolic ward, where every single thing they ate could be measured precisely and nobody could sneak a snack.
Each person spent two weeks on an ultra-processed diet and two weeks on an unprocessed diet, in random order, so each person served as their own control.
And, critically, the two diets were carefully matched for total calories offered, sugar, fat, saturated fat, salt, fibre and macronutrients.
On paper, nutritionally, they were the same diet.
The only difference was processing.
Participants were told to eat as much or as little as they wanted at every meal.
On the ultra-processed diet, people ate about five hundred calories a day more than on the unprocessed diet.
Same nutrients on offer.
Same people.
Five hundred extra calories a day, spontaneously, without noticing.
Over the two weeks they gained roughly a kilogram.
On the unprocessed diet, the same people lost roughly a kilogram.
That result is the keystone of the whole argument, because it is a randomised controlled trial, not an observational correlation, and it says the processing itself does something.
Nutritionism, the habit of reducing food to a list of numbers on a label, cannot explain it.
So what is the mechanism?
Van Tulleken walks through the leading explanations, and they are more interesting than a simple story about sugar.
The first is speed.
In Hall's study, one of the clearest differences was that people ate the ultra-processed meals faster.
Ultra-processed food is soft.
It has been, in van Tulleken's phrase, pre-chewed.

The industrial processes that make it, the extrusion, the milling to fine powders, the emulsification, break down the physical structure of the original ingredients, what scientists call the food matrix.
Real food resists you.
It requires work, and that work takes time.
Your satiety signalling system, the hormonal conversation between your gut and your brain, is slow, and it evolved in a world where eating was slow too.
If you can deliver a thousand calories in six minutes with almost no chewing, you will be finished long before your body has any idea what has happened.
Add energy density to that.
Because water and fibre have been removed and fat and refined starch added, ultra-processed food packs far more calories into each mouthful.
Fast eating plus dense calories is a combination that defeats the appetite system by simply outrunning it.
Then there is what the destruction of the matrix does to the nutrition itself.

Whole almonds and almond flour contain the same nutrients on a label and behave very differently in a human gut, because in the whole nut a substantial amount of the fat stays locked in cell walls and passes through undigested.
Grinding it releases it all.
The label does not change.
The reality does.
The second cluster of mechanisms concerns the additives, and van Tulleken is careful here, because the science is younger and he is a scientist by training.
He is not claiming these substances are poisons.
He is making a narrower and more troubling point.
Take emulsifiers, the compounds that keep oil and water from separating and give products a creamy mouthfeel and a long shelf life.

Researchers including Benoit Chassaing and Andrew Gewirtz have fed common emulsifiers such as polysorbate eighty and carboxymethylcellulose to mice at doses meant to be relevant to human consumption, and observed changes in the gut microbiome, thinning of the protective mucus layer that keeps bacteria at arm's length from the intestinal wall, low-grade inflammation, and features of metabolic syndrome.
Human work has since begun and points in a similar direction, though it is early.
Take non-sugar sweeteners.

Work from the Weizmann Institute in Israel by Eran Elinav and Eran Segal found that certain sweeteners could alter the gut microbiome in ways that impaired glucose tolerance in mice, and in a subset of human volunteers.
Again, early, contested, and not a proof of harm at population scale.
But not nothing.
The deeper point van Tulleken keeps returning to is about how these substances are approved.
Additives are generally tested individually, at specified doses, for specific acute harms, usually by or on behalf of the companies that want to use them.
They are not tested in the combinations in which people actually consume them, dozens at a time, from dozens of products, every day, for eighty years, starting in infancy.
Nobody has run that trial, and nobody is going to.
So when he says we are running an uncontrolled experiment on the population, he is not being rhetorical.
He is describing the regulatory situation accurately.
The third mechanism is the one the industry spends the most money on, and it is flavour engineering.
Ultra-processed food is not accidentally delicious.

It is designed, by teams of sensory scientists with laboratories and panels and enormous datasets, to hit the precise point of maximum appeal, what the food scientist Howard Moskowitz famously called the bliss point.
The mix of sugar, salt, fat and aroma that produces the strongest craving is not the mix that produces the strongest satisfaction.
Those are different targets, and industry aims at the first.
There is a related trick that van Tulleken finds particularly revealing, which the food scientist Steven Witherly described as vanishing caloric density.
A cheese puff dissolves almost instantly on the tongue.

Your brain, which learns how calorific a food is partly through the experience of chewing and swallowing, receives a signal that this thing has essentially no substance, and therefore never registers a stopping point.
So you can eat the whole bag and feel, genuinely, that you have eaten nothing.
There is also the deliberate defeat of sensory-specific satiety.
Your appetite for a particular flavour fades as you eat it, which is why the fifth spoonful of plain porridge is much less appealing than the first.
It is one of the body's oldest brakes, and it exists to make you eat a varied diet.
Products engineered with complex, shifting flavour profiles blunt that brake, so the twentieth crisp tastes as interesting as the first.
There is a fourth mechanism that gets less attention and may matter as much as the others: what this food does not contain.
Ultra-processed food is, almost by definition, low in fibre, because fibre is removed during refining and is inconvenient in manufacturing.
And fibre is not merely roughage.

It is the food supply for the trillions of bacteria in your large intestine, which ferment it into short-chain fatty acids that feed the cells lining your gut, regulate inflammation, and participate in appetite signalling.
Starve that population and you change an organ.

Van Tulleken's framing is that we have not simply added strange molecules to the diet, we have simultaneously subtracted the substrate that an entire internal ecosystem runs on, and we did it inside a single human lifetime.
He also spends time on why the nutrition advice we were given for fifty years was so useless, and the history is genuinely scandalous.
For decades the public argument was framed as fat versus sugar, and it was not a purely scientific argument.

Documents unearthed by researchers showed that in the nineteen sixties the Sugar Research Foundation paid Harvard scientists to produce a review in a leading medical journal that downplayed sugar's role in heart disease and pointed the finger at fat, without the funding being disclosed.

The consequences were enormous, because when fat became the villain, the food industry responded by producing tens of thousands of low-fat products, and removing fat from food makes it taste of very little, so the fat was replaced with sugar, starch, thickeners and flavourings.
In other words, the single largest piece of public health advice of the twentieth century functioned, in practice, as a marketing brief for ultra-processed food.
That is the deeper reason van Tulleken wants to move the conversation away from nutrients altogether.
Every time we identify a villain molecule, the industry reformulates around it and sells us the reformulation as health.
Low fat gave us more sugar.
Low sugar gave us sweeteners.
Now high protein is giving us protein isolates and bars with twenty ingredients.
The category keeps winning because the question keeps being asked at the level of the molecule rather than the level of the product.
Which brings us to the question the book handles most carefully.
Is this stuff addictive?
Van Tulleken's position is that the argument about whether food can be addictive has often been a semantic distraction.
What he does instead is take the standard clinical criteria used to define a substance use disorder and hold them up against how people actually behave with ultra-processed food.
Consuming more than intended.
Persistent desire and unsuccessful attempts to cut down.
Continued use despite clear physical or psychological harm.
Craving.
Withdrawal-like symptoms.
Tolerance.
Giving up other activities.
Researchers including Ashley Gearhardt at Michigan have built and validated scales along exactly these lines, and a substantial fraction of people meet the threshold with respect to certain foods.
Van Tulleken's own experience during his experiment is his evidence in chief.

He knew precisely what he was eating, he knew exactly what it was doing to his body, he had access to the world's best information and every possible motivation to stop, and he was still standing in a kitchen at eleven at night eating something he did not want.
He is explicit about the moral consequence he draws.
If this stuff produces compulsive consumption in people who understand it completely, then the framing of obesity as a failure of individual willpower is not just unkind.
It is factually wrong, and it is also, and this is the part that sharpens the book, an argument with a documented origin.
Because here is where van Tulleken makes his most pointed historical case.
The modern ultra-processed food industry and the tobacco industry are not merely similar in their tactics.
For a period, they were substantially the same companies.
In the nineteen eighties, Philip Morris, the maker of Marlboro, bought General Foods and then Kraft, becoming for a while the largest food company in the United States.
R J Reynolds, the tobacco company, merged with Nabisco.
Executives, scientists, flavour chemists and marketers moved between the divisions.

And because of the litigation settlements of the nineteen nineties, the internal documents of the tobacco industry are now public and searchable, which means researchers have been able to trace what happened next.

They have documented flavour technology and consumer-psychology research developed for cigarettes being applied to food products, and the same marketing frameworks, including the targeting of children and of particular communities, moving across.
The playbook moved too.
Fund research that produces doubt.
Emphasise that the science is not settled.
Establish front organisations that look like scientific bodies.
Sponsor the professional associations of the people who advise the public.
Fund physical activity campaigns so that the conversation becomes about exercise rather than product.
And above all, relentlessly reframe a systemic problem as a matter of personal responsibility and individual choice, because a person who blames themselves does not campaign for regulation.
On the corruption of the science, van Tulleken is specific and he includes himself in the indictment.

He describes the International Life Sciences Institute, founded by a Coca-Cola executive, which for decades presented itself as a neutral scientific body while shaping nutrition policy around the world.
He notes the major dietetic and nutrition professional bodies that have taken sponsorship from the manufacturers of the products under discussion.
He goes through the research showing that industry-funded nutrition studies are substantially more likely to produce conclusions favourable to the sponsor.

And, to his credit, he discloses his own entanglements, including work he has done that was funded in ways he now regards as compromised, and a period during which he says he was, in effect, part of the machinery.
There is a chapter on infant feeding that is the angriest in the book, and it is worth knowing about.

Van Tulleken describes breast milk as an extraordinary living fluid, containing components that the baby cannot digest at all and which exist purely to feed and shape the infant's gut microbiome, along with immune cells and antibodies that adjust to the baby's environment.

He then walks through the history of breast milk substitute marketing, including the Nestlé scandal and the World Health Organization code that followed, and argues that the aggressive marketing of formula, and now of ultra-processed toddler foods and fruit pouches, represents one of the clearest cases of a commercial product displacing something better and being sold on the basis of parental anxiety.
He is careful, and this matters, to say repeatedly that the failure is not the parents'.
Many parents cannot breastfeed, and many more are given no support to do so, and shame is both cruel and useless.
His target is the marketing and the policy, not the mother at three in the morning with a bottle.
So what does all this do to a population over time?
Here the evidence is observational rather than experimental, and van Tulleken says so, but the volume of it is considerable.

Very large cohort studies, including the French NutriNet-Santé study following well over a hundred thousand people, have found consistent associations between the proportion of ultra-processed food in the diet and a long list of outcomes.
In that study a ten percent increase in the proportion of ultra-processed food in the diet was associated with roughly a twelve percent increase in overall cancer risk.

Other cohorts and umbrella reviews have linked higher ultra-processed consumption to cardiovascular disease, type two diabetes, obesity, depression, inflammatory bowel disease, frailty in older people, cognitive decline, and all-cause mortality.

Associations are not proof of causation, and he is honest that people who eat a great deal of ultra-processed food differ from those who do not in many ways, including income, and that statistical adjustment is imperfect.

What he argues is that the combination of consistent epidemiology across many countries and populations, plus a randomised trial showing a causal effect on intake, plus a set of plausible mechanisms, is exactly the pattern of evidence that eventually convinced the world about tobacco, and that waiting for perfect proof has a body count.
One of the sharpest sections in the book concerns labelling, because it is where the industry's stated position and its revealed position diverge most visibly.
Manufacturers say, consistently and in public, that they support consumer choice and consumer information.

And then, over decades and across many countries, industry bodies have lobbied hard against simple front-of-pack schemes, the colour-coded traffic lights, the Chilean-style black warning octagons, the Nutri-Score letter grades, on grounds that these are unscientific, oversimplified or unfair to individual products.
Van Tulleken's read is that the objection is not really to inaccuracy.
The objection is that these labels work.
In Chile, where mandatory black warning labels were combined with restrictions on marketing to children and on selling those products in schools, purchases of the labelled products fell measurably.
A label that changes behaviour is, from a commercial standpoint, a problem to be managed.
The same logic runs through the marketing to children, which he treats as the least defensible part of the entire system.

Advertising works best on people whose capacity to evaluate persuasive intent is not yet developed, which is the definition of a small child, and the products advertised to children are almost entirely from group four.

Cartoon characters, toy tie-ins, school sponsorships, sports partnerships, and now enormous volumes of influencer and in-game marketing that sits well outside the reach of broadcast advertising rules written in another era.

He points out the obvious asymmetry: a parent making a decision in a supermarket aisle is up against a budget of many millions and a team of behavioural specialists, and the parent is then told the outcome reflects their choices.
And then there is the argument that comes up whenever any of this is raised, which is that people should simply cook.
Van Tulleken takes it seriously and then dismantles it in the only way that counts, with practicalities.

Cooking from group one ingredients requires equipment, storage, a working freezer, transport to a shop that sells fresh food at reasonable prices, a stable enough schedule to shop and prepare, energy at the end of a shift, and skills that have to be learned from somebody.
Substantial numbers of households in Britain and America are short of several of those at once.
Ultra-processed food is not merely cheaper per calorie, it is cheaper per unit of time and effort and risk, it does not go off, and a child will reliably eat it.

He notes that in poorer households the wasted cost of a rejected meal is not a minor inconvenience but a real financial event, which makes the guaranteed acceptability of engineered food a rational thing to buy.
He is also honest about his own position while making this argument.

He is a well-paid doctor in London with a functioning kitchen and time to think about food, and he says plainly that a message which works for him and does not work for a person on a zero-hours contract with two children and a broken oven is not a public health policy.
It is a lifestyle preference with a scientific vocabulary.
There is one more strand, which is why this food exists at all in these quantities, and the answer is economics.
Ultra-processed food is built from a small number of extremely cheap commodity crops, principally maize, soy, wheat and palm oil, which are grown at enormous scale and often subsidised.
Those commodities are fractionated into starches, oils, protein isolates and syrups, which are then reassembled, with additives, into a near infinite range of products.
The result is food that is cheap per calorie, extraordinarily shelf-stable, transportable, brandable and enormously profitable, in a way that a carrot can never be.
Nobody advertises carrots because nobody owns carrots.
That structure has consequences beyond human health.
The demand for palm oil and soy drives deforestation.
The system is highly concentrated among a small number of very large corporations.

And it makes ultra-processed food, for a great many people, not the easy choice but the only affordable and accessible one, which is why van Tulleken keeps insisting that this is a question of policy rather than personal virtue.
There is a particularly neat trap that follows from all of this, which van Tulleken calls out and which is worth naming because most of us have fallen into it.
The same industry that manufactures the products associated with weight gain also manufactures, and profits enormously from, the products sold as the solution.
Diet versions, meal replacement shakes, low-calorie ready meals, sweetener-laden zero drinks, high-protein bars, slimming ranges.

Almost all of them are, by the NOVA definition, squarely group four, and several of them require more additives than the original product they replace, because removing sugar or fat from a formulation creates a hole that has to be filled with something.

So a person trying to eat better is very often moved from one ultra-processed product to another ultra-processed product, at a higher price, with a health claim on the front, and when it does not work they conclude the failure is theirs.
Van Tulleken's point is not that every such product is harmful.
It is that an industry which sells you both the problem and the cure has no commercial interest in you resolving either, and that this is a structural feature rather than a conspiracy.
It is simply what a market does when the same companies own both shelves.
And that leads to his ending, which is unusual, and which I want to be honest about because it will either please you or frustrate you.
He does not give you a diet plan.
He refuses to, explicitly and on principle.

His view is that telling individuals to simply stop eating ultra-processed food, when it is the cheapest, most available, most heavily marketed food in the country and is engineered to be difficult to stop eating, is like telling people in a polluted city to breathe less.

The real solutions he argues for are structural: marketing restrictions, especially to children, honest and mandatory front-of-pack labelling, an end to industry funding of nutrition science and of the bodies that advise governments, taxation and subsidy that changes relative prices, and treating the sector the way tobacco eventually came to be treated.
But he does offer one personal practice, and it is more interesting than a rule.
He suggests you eat as much ultra-processed food as you like, on one condition: read the packet first, and understand what you are reading.
Look up the additives.
Learn what the emulsifier is for.
Notice that the ingredient list contains fourteen things that were made in a factory to make a cheap substrate resemble food.
His claim, based on what happened to him, is that this knowledge is not neutral information.
It changes desire.
Over the course of researching and writing the book, van Tulleken did not quit ultra-processed food by an act of discipline.
He stopped wanting it, gradually, as understanding accumulated, in roughly the way that a person who learns exactly what is in a cigarette tends to enjoy it less.
He frames it as informed consent rather than restriction, and he thinks it works better than willpower because it does not rely on willpower at all.
If you want a picture of what a sane alternative looks like, van Tulleken points to Brazil, which is fitting given where the whole idea came from.
Brazil's national dietary guidelines, written with Carlos Monteiro's involvement, are unlike almost any other country's.
They do not lead with grams of saturated fat or a pyramid of food groups.

The central instruction is to make natural or minimally processed foods the basis of your diet, to use oils, fats, salt and sugar in small amounts when cooking, to limit processed foods, and to avoid ultra-processed foods.
But the part people quote is the rest of it, because it is not about nutrients at all.
Eat regularly and carefully, in appropriate environments, and whenever possible in company.
Develop, exercise and share cooking skills.
Plan your time to give food the space it deserves.
When you eat out, choose places that make food on the premises.
And be wary of food advertising and marketing, which the guidelines name explicitly as a thing to defend yourself against, in a government document.

Van Tulleken clearly loves this, because it treats eating as a cultural and social act rather than a chemistry problem, and because it names the commercial pressure openly instead of pretending the consumer is operating in a vacuum.
Whether a set of guidelines can hold back a global industry is another question, and Brazil's own consumption of ultra-processed food has continued to rise.
But it is at least an example of a country writing down what it actually knows.
Now let me give you the honest caveats, because a good summary owes you them.
The NOVA classification has real critics.

Some nutrition scientists argue that the ultra-processed category is too broad, lumping a fizzy drink together with a wholegrain supermarket loaf and a fortified plant milk, and that this makes it a blunt instrument for policy.

Some argue that the associations in cohort studies are largely explained by the sugar, salt, fat and low fibre of these foods after all, and that Hall's trial, while excellent, involved twenty people for two weeks and needs replication at scale, which is now underway.

And there is a genuine risk that a message about food purity becomes a new source of shame for people who cannot afford or access an alternative, which van Tulleken is alert to and works hard to avoid.
None of that undoes the central case.

Something in the way we now manufacture food causes people to eat significantly more of it than they otherwise would, and that effect has been demonstrated under controlled conditions, and the food that does this now constitutes the majority of the British and American diet, and it arrived there through a commercial system with a documented history of exactly this behaviour in another product category.
So let me pull it together.
A Brazilian researcher noticed that families were buying less sugar while getting fatter, and realised the sugar had moved inside the packet.

That produced a way of classifying food not by its nutrients but by how far it has been taken from food, and the fourth category, ultra-processed, now describes about sixty percent of what the English-speaking world eats.
A doctor ate that ordinary diet for four weeks and gained six kilograms, disrupted his appetite hormones, and grew new connections between the habit and reward centres of his brain.
A metabolic ward trial then showed that when you match two diets on every nutrient and vary only the processing, people spontaneously eat five hundred extra calories a day on the processed one.
The mechanisms are not mysterious.
The food is soft, so you eat it fast.
It is dense, so each mouthful carries more.
Its structure has been destroyed, so your gut absorbs it differently than the label suggests.
Its flavour is engineered to the point of maximum craving rather than maximum satisfaction, and to defeat the natural brake that makes you tire of a taste.

And it carries a cocktail of additives tested one at a time, for short periods, by the people who wish to sell them, and never in the combination in which a human being actually consumes them across a lifetime.

And the reason it is everywhere is that it is enormously profitable to convert four subsidised commodity crops into branded, shelf-stable products, and because the industry that does this learned its marketing, its lobbying and its science-funding strategy in part from the tobacco business, sometimes inside the very same corporations.
Van Tulleken's conclusion is not that you are weak.
It is that you are the target of an extremely well-resourced and highly competent effort, and that the appropriate response to that is not shame but information, and then politics.
So let me leave you with the practical heart of it, the things you can do this week.
Start reading ingredient lists, not nutrition panels, and use the plastic wrapper test: if it contains something you would never find in a domestic kitchen, you are holding ultra-processed food.
Do this for a week without changing what you buy.
Just look.
That alone is his primary intervention.

Look particularly hard at the products you assume are healthy, because low-fat, low-sugar, high-protein and plant-based reformulations usually require more additives, not fewer, and the health halo is doing work that the ingredients are not.
Slow your eating down, deliberately, because speed is one of the clearest mechanisms in the evidence.
Put the fork down between mouthfuls, and notice how much of your food requires almost no chewing at all.
Shift one habitual purchase at a time rather than attempting a full conversion.
Bread, breakfast and snacks are where most people's ultra-processed calories are concentrated, so start there, and accept that this is easier for some budgets and schedules than others.
Cook things that make more than one meal, because time and money are the real constraints, and any strategy that ignores them will fail by Wednesday.

Be sceptical of nutrition advice without checking who funded it, including advice from professional bodies, charities and researchers, and treat industry sponsorship as relevant information rather than a technicality.
And drop the willpower framing entirely, for yourself and for everyone else.
A person eating a packet of something engineered by sensory scientists to defeat their satiety signalling is not failing a character test.
Knowing that is not an excuse.
It is the first accurate piece of information most of us have ever been given about our own appetites.
